case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

[Core Objective]

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.

[Case]
A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).
